contributions: A drop-in change to the critic's learning objective only — the actor loss, advantage estimation, rollout pipeline, optimizer and evaluation are held fixed, so differences are attributable to critic parameterization rather than to a new training recipe

An explicit refusal to claim the distributional framing does the work: the categorical output is never passed to the actor, only its decoded expectation, so this is a training surrogate rather than a distributional policy-improvement algorithm

Two candidate optimization mechanisms stated as plausible rather than proved — a broader per-sample gradient channel through a multi-output head, and better-conditioned local geometry from keeping targets away from the simplex corners where the Fisher information matrix degenerates

Controls that rule out the cheap explanations: a Bernoulli two-bin critic isolates binary classification, and a one-hot categorical head with the same output dimensionality isolates head capacity from target smoothing
Direct calibration and advantage-distribution measurements against an oracle success probability estimated from 256 Monte Carlo continuations per prefix
limitations: The paper states them and they are the right ones. Backbone coverage is the Qwen family at 4B to 7B, so broader architectures and larger models are untested. The calibration and advantage analyses are diagnostic and do not establish that advantage symmetry is the only causal mediator of the policy gains — the paper repeats this refusal in three separate places rather than letting the correlation stand as a mechanism. The best support margins and smoothing bandwidth can depend on a task's reward range, with sensitivity deferred to the appendix. Two things a reader should add. The gradient-channel argument is explicitly noted to be generic to any multi-output head and is contradicted as a sufficient explanation by the authors' own one-hot result, so it survives only as one of two partial accounts. And no seeds or variance are reported for the main tables, which matters less here than in most papers of this shape because the controls, not the margin, carry the argument — but the 2.86-point avg@256 headline is still a single number from a single run.
method: The critic's final linear projection to a scalar becomes an m-way linear layer with a softmax over bins evenly spaced across a fixed value range; the scalar estimate is the expectation of that distribution and is what GAE consumes. Each training step's bootstrapped return is projected onto the bins by the HL-Gauss rule, giving each bin the Gaussian CDF mass falling within it, and the critic minimizes cross-entropy against that target over valid response tokens. The actor keeps the standard clipped surrogate. The PPO baseline is deliberately strong rather than vanilla, incorporating DAPO and parts of the VAPO recipe — Clip-Higher, token-level loss, critic pretraining and group sampling — applied uniformly to every critic variant, with lambda set to 1. Backbones are Qwen2.5-Math-7B for mathematics, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for tool-augmented mathematics and Search-R1, and Qwen3-4B-Base as a generalization check, trained on DAPO-Math-17K under verl. Advantage dynamics are probed by collecting 64 rollouts per problem on AIME24 and AIME25, and calibration by scoring four positions per rollout against an oracle success probability from 256 Monte Carlo continuations.
one_liner: Replaces PPO's scalar mean-squared-error critic head with a categorical predictor over a discretized value support trained by cross-entropy against Gaussian-smoothed targets, decodes it back to a scalar for an unchanged GAE update, and shows the resulting critic is better calibrated and produces near-symmetric advantages where the MSE critic penalizes failures two-to-three times harder than it rewards successes.
problem: In RLVR with binary terminal rewards, the return from an intermediate state is Bernoulli and its conditional mean is the probability of eventual success, so scalar MSE regression is statistically consistent for exactly the quantity PPO needs — the paper is explicit that scalar critics are not representationally invalid. The problem is optimization and calibration. The critic enters the actor update as a subtraction, so a modest value error becomes a systematically asymmetric learning signal: if the critic overestimates success probability, failed rollouts receive large negative advantages while successful ones receive small positive ones, and the policy update spends most of its magnitude on failures.

relevance.reasoning-training: It identifies a failure in outcome-supervised RL that is invisible in the reward and lives entirely in the critic: with a binary terminal reward the advantage is the reward minus the value estimate, so a miscalibrated value turns a symmetric reward into an asymmetric learning signal, and the measured ratio is 2.63 to 2.78 against failures. That is a concrete mechanism for something this archive keeps observing indirectly — that outcome-only training pushes policies away from failure faster than toward success, with entropy collapse and narrowed pass@k as downstream symptoms. The paper also demonstrates the diagnostic that would catch it, which is not a benchmark number: measure the mean advantage conditioned on outcome and take the ratio, where 1.0 is symmetric learning. Its experimental discipline is worth copying too. The one-hot control, which underperforms the scalar baseline it was meant to improve on, is what turns 'classification helps' into the narrower and more useful 'smoothed targets help, and a bigger head on its own hurts'.

results: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B the average avg@256 across five mathematics benchmarks rises from 15.88 for PPO and 16.00 for DAPO to 18.74, and pass@256 from 38.48 and 42.34 to 48.06 — a 9.58-point gain, larger than the 2.86 on avg@256, which the paper explains through the sensitivity of pass@k to improvements on low-probability problems. Worth noting in passing: PPO's pass@256 of 38.48 sits below the untrained base model's 40.74, so the baseline narrows the reasoning boundary and the categorical critic recovers past it. The trend holds on Qwen3-4B-Base (15.33 to 17.18 and 53.40 to 57.13) and on Search-R1 with a different backbone, where the seven-dataset mean@1 average rises from 44.91 to 47.13 with every individual dataset positive. The controls are what make the claim specific. A Bernoulli two-bin critic improves pass@256 over MSE (45.67 against 38.48) but not avg@256 (15.50 against 15.88), so binary classification recovers rare successful trajectories without accounting for the rest. A one-hot categorical head with the same dimensionality is worse than MSE on avg@256 (14.86), so a multi-output head alone is insufficient; two-hot reaches 17.55 and full smoothing 18.74, placing the benefit on target construction. The advantage statistics are the sharpest evidence: on AIME24 the MSE critic gives failed rollouts a mean advantage of -0.597 against +0.227 for successes, a ratio of 2.63, while HL-Gauss gives -0.466 against +0.458, a ratio of 1.02, with the same pattern on AIME25 (2.78 against 0.99). The paper notes correctly that batch-wise advantage normalization is an affine rescaling and does not remove this relative asymmetry, and that the MSE ratio grows more skewed over training steps while HL-Gauss stays near one. Calibration improves in step: Brier 0.2031 to 0.1637, ECE 0.2612 to 0.2131, MCE 0.4191 to 0.3021, with the largest gap in the region where the oracle probability is below 0.5 — exactly where overestimation inflates negative advantages.
